slides.title: Operations - Lookup
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Operations - Lookup

Lookup a search key within the Bt-tree:

1

start with the root node

2

is the current node a leaf?

> if yes, return the current page (locate the entry on it)

find the first entry > search key (binary search)

if no such entry is found, go the upper, otherwise go to the corresponding page

continue with 2

Lookup can return a concrete entry or just the position on the appropriate leaf page (depends

on usage pattern).

slides.title: Operations - Insert
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Operations - Insert

Insert a new entry into the Bt-tree:

lookup the appropriate leaf page

is there free space on the leaf?

> if yes, insert entry and stop

split the leaf into two, insert entry on proper side

insert maximum of left page as separator into parent

if the parent overflow, split parent and continue with 4

create a new root if needed

slides.title: Operations - Delete
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Operations - Delete

Remove an entry from the Bt-tree:

1

lookup the appropriate leaf page

2

remove the entry from the current page

3

is the current page at least half full?

> if yes, stop

4. is the neighboring page more than half full?

P if yes, balance both pages, update separator, and stop

merge neighboring page into current page

remove the separator from the parent, continue with 3

Most systems simplify the delete logic and accept under-full pages

slides.title: Operations - Range Scan
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Operations - Range Scan

Read all entries within a (start,stop( range

lookup the start value

enumerate subsequent entries on the current page

use the next pointer to find the next page

stop once the stop value is reached

Very efficient, in particular if leaf nodes are consecutive on disk

slides.title: Concurrent Access
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Concurrent Access

How to handle concurrent access?

e simple page locking/latching is not enough

e will protect against “simple” (single page) changes

e but pages depend upon each other (pointers)

The classical technique is lock coupling

e

a thread latches both the page and its parent page

e

i.e., latch the root, latch the first level, release the root, latch the second level etc

e

prevents conflicts, as pages can only be split when the parent is latched

no deadlocks, as the latches are ordered

slides.title: Concurrent Access (2)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Concurrent Access (2)

But what about inserts?

e when a leaf is split, the separator is propagated up

¢ might go up to the root

e but we have only locked one parent

Lock coupling up is not an option (deadlocks)

One way around it: “safe” inner pages

e while going down, check if the inner page has enough space

for one more entry

e if not, split it

e ensures that we never go up more than one step

slides.title: Concurrent Access (3)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Concurrent Access (3)

Alternative: restart

1

first try to insert using simple lock coupling

2

if we do not have to split the inner node everything is fine

3

otherwise release all latches

restart the operation, but now keep all latches up to the root

all operations can be executed safely now

© greatly reduces concurrency

e but should happen rarely

e simpler to implement, in particular for variable-length keys

slides.title: B-link Trees
slides.slide_text_ocr:
B-link Trees

e lock coupling latches two nodes at a time

e seems cheap, but effectively it locks hundreds (all children of the parent node)

e it would be nicer to lock only one page

For pure lookups that is possible when adding next pointers to inner nodes:

1. latch a page, find the child page, release the page

2. latch the child page

3. might have been split in between, check neighboring pages

Requires some care when deleting.

slides.title: Bulkloading
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Bulkloading

How to build an B-tree for a large amount of data?

e repeated inserts are inefficient

¢ a lot of random |/O

¢ pages are touched multiple times

Instead: sort the data before inserting

e now inserts become more efficient

e good locality

But we can do even better.

slides.title: Bulkloading (2)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Bulkloading (2)

To construct an initial Bt-Tree:

1. sort the data

2. spool data into leaf pages

> fill the pages completely

> remember largest value (separator) in each page in a temp file

3. spool the separators into inner pages

> fill the pages completely

> remember largest value (separator) in each page in a temp file

4. repeat 3 until only one inner page remains (root)

Produces a compact, clustered Bt-tree.

slides.title: Bulkloading (3)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Bulkloading (3)

Existing B*-trees are a bit more problematic, but can still be updated in bulk

1

sort the data

merge the data into the existing tree

form pages, remember separators, etc.

start a new chunk once a page would contain only entries from the original tree

merge in the separators as above

Minimizes 1/O, but destroys clustering. Usually a good compromise.

slides.title: Variable Length Records (3)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Variable Length Records (3)

Separator choice is crucial!

e affects fanout and space consumption

e all standard guarantees are off if normal algorithms are used for variable-length keys

Non-trivial issue

e greedy algorithms exist for the bulkloading case

e idea: recursively pick the smallest value as separator such that the resulting group sizes

vary within a constant factor

e can also be extended to the dynamic case (rebuild as need), but non-trivial

e difficult, but gives good amortized bounds

slides.title: Variable Length Records (4)
slides.slide_text_ocr:
Variable Length Records (4)

Minimal support: modify the split logic

1. when a page overflows, build the sorted list of all values

2. instead of picking the median value as separator, pick the smallest value within 20% around

the median

3. for ties, prefer values closer to the median

e pragmatic solution, but not optimal

e can still degenerate

e avoids the worst mistakes
